strengths: Novel perspective investigating brain predictive coding from decoding rather than encoding perspective
Comprehensive experimental analysis including ROI ablations, prediction distance analysis, information loss quantification, and detailed error analysis
Well-motivated predictive coding verification experiment that demonstrates correlation between LM representations and brain responses in specific ROIs
Sound technical methodology with appropriate use of FIR models for BOLD delay compensation and proper dataset splitting to avoid data leakage
Insightful contribution regarding temporal information loss problem in fMRI and how predictive coding may help mitigate it
Clear presentation with well-designed visualizations of model architecture and experimental results
weaknesses: Low absolute performance despite improvements: BLEU-1 only reaches 27.8%, BLEU-2/3/4 remain critically low (<3%), suggesting models cannot generate coherent multi-word phrases
Severely limited experimental scope: single dataset (Narratives), only one direct baseline comparison (UniCoRN), no per-subject splitting experiments
Weak theoretical-empirical connection: prediction scores in verification are small (~0.005); unclear why encoding-perspective predictive coding findings drive decoding improvements

Mechanism remains opaque: no analysis of why prediction distance d=4 is optimal, whether improvements come specifically from predictive coding vs. auxiliary supervision, or which predictions actually contribute

Questionable architectural choices: cross-attention mask allows future predictions to attend to current tokens (causally backward), variable λ hyperparameter suggests dataset-specific tuning, stop gradient on embeddings unexplained
Reproducibility concerns: no code availability mentioned, hyperparameter choices lack justification, no error bars or significance tests on main results
No sensitivity analysis for critical design choices: fixed window length l=2, choice of 6 ROIs, architectural differences between networks (P=4/Q=12 vs M=N=6)

strengths: Well-motivated connection to brain predictive coding theory with validation experiment in Section 2
Comprehensive experimental analysis including novel information loss slope metric and detailed error distribution analysis
Clear methodology and transparent presentation of model architecture with ablation studies demonstrating side network contribution
Consistent improvements over UniCoRN baseline across multiple metrics and sequence lengths
Thorough investigation of ROI selection effects and prediction distance, showing specificity of brain predictive coding regions
weaknesses: Limited architectural novelty: components (3D CNN, FIR, Transformer, cross-attention) are standard; contribution is primarily application-level rather than methodological

Weak theoretical validation: paper shows correlation between LM activations and brain responses (Section 2) but doesn't rigorously justify why this specific architecture exploits predictive coding, nor isolate predictive coding contribution from improved features
Insufficient baselines: only UniCoRN compared; dismissal of Tang et al. [33] and Ye et al. [42] as incompatible is insufficient; no diagnostic baselines to test core claims
Limited scope: single dataset (Narratives), cross-subject splitting only, fixed window length l=2 due to computational constraints, undermining generalization claims
Modest absolute improvements with questionable practical significance: BLEU-1 improvement of ~6 points, but BLEU-2/3/4 remain extremely low (≤2%); case study shows output remains incoherent

Information loss analysis (Appendix B) reveals fundamental data limitation rather than validating method; no principled explanation for why predictive coding helps with temporal resolution mismatch; confounds predictive coding with context provision

Side network contribution not mechanistically explained: unclear whether improvements come from predictive coding vs. simply using better linguistic ROI features; no visualization or analysis of what side network learns

Unresolved theoretical contradiction: paper cites Antonello & Huth [2] questioning whether LMs fit brain data through prediction, but doesn't address why decoding should benefit from encoding-level insights

strengths: Well-motivated investigation of brain predictive coding from the decoding perspective with convincing verification experiment (Section 2)
Comprehensive experimental analysis including novel ROI selection experiments, prediction distance analysis, and information loss slope metric that provide clear insights
Rigorous methodology addressing known data leakage issues with proper cross-subject splitting and appropriate preprocessing choices
Thorough ablation studies and error analysis demonstrating the side network's effectiveness and revealing systematic information loss patterns in fMRI decoding
Technically sound model architecture with clear presentation, proper FIR modeling of BOLD delay, and well-formalized attention mechanisms
Honest acknowledgment of limitations including single-dataset evaluation and fundamental fMRI temporal resolution constraints
weaknesses: Limited architectural novelty—the core contribution is applying standard Transformer components (side network with self-attention and cross-attention fusion) rather than methodological innovation, making it incremental for NLP venues
Single-dataset evaluation (Narratives only) severely limits generalizability claims; authors acknowledge but don't address this critical gap
Incomplete baseline comparisons—only compared to UniCoRN; Tang et al. [33] and Ye et al. [42] dismissed on compatibility grounds, raising concerns about selective comparisons

Very low absolute performance on higher-order n-grams (BLEU-2/3/4: 8.29%, 2.0%, 0.54% at length=40) and incoherent case studies (Table 3), questioning practical utility and significance of improvements
Modest improvements in key metrics (e.g., ROUGE1-R 19.53% vs 19.76% for UniCoRN at length=40) without statistical significance testing; precision-recall trade-offs unexplained
Theory-practice gap: while brain predictive coding is verified at encoding level, the mechanism by which encoding-level predictions improve autoregressive generation is not adequately explained

Design choices insufficiently justified: l=2 window length limited by computational resources, d=4 optimal prediction distance lacks principled explanation, hyperparameter λ varies across sequence lengths without clear justification
Missing ablations on different ROI sources, per-subject analysis, attention weight interpretation, and robustness testing; no code release mentioned

strengths: Well-motivated interdisciplinary approach connecting neuroscience predictive coding theory to fMRI-to-text decoding with theoretical grounding
Comprehensive experimental validation including verification experiment, within/cross-subject evaluation, ablations, ROI analysis, and systematic prediction length/distance studies
Consistent empirical improvements over strong baselines (34.95% BLEU-1 vs 27.11% MapGuide within-subject; 27.8% vs 21.76% UniCoRN cross-subject)
Sound methodology with detailed reproducibility information, proper train/test splitting, and public datasets
Thorough error analysis (Appendix D) revealing information loss patterns and demonstrating PREDFT's mitigation capability
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: architecture combines standard components (3D CNN, FIR, Transformer) without significant innovation; attention fusion (Eq. 4) is conventional

Unresolved causal inference: verification experiment establishes correlation but not that prediction specifically (rather than better ROI selection) improves decoding; alternative explanations unaddressed
Modest absolute performance: BLEU-4 drops to 1.78%, case study shows incoherent output; improvements mainly capture semantic concepts rather than fluent sequences
Dataset/generalization limitations: LeBel's has only 3 subjects; ROI selection depends on prior knowledge; different configurations per dataset reduce transferability
Fundamental fMRI ceiling: information loss problem is hardware-inherent; φ score reduction (0.86→0.64) shows remaining degradation persists regardless of model improvements

Evaluation gaps: no statistical significance testing reported; BERTScore shows marginal gains (82.92 vs 82.66); no human evaluation despite acknowledged metric limitations; limited case study (2 examples)
Incomplete analysis: why medium prediction length (l=4-6) optimal unexplored; biological interpretation missing; minimal investigation of which linguistic phenomena benefit from prediction
Methodological sensitivity: hyperparameter λ requires dataset-specific tuning; multi-task loss L=L_Main+λL_Side is simplistic; architectural choices (layer counts) unjustified

strengths: Well-grounded in neuroscience theory (predictive coding) with preliminary verification experiments
Comprehensive experimental analysis across two datasets with extensive supplementary studies and ablations
Consistent empirical improvements over baselines on multiple evaluation metrics (BLEU, ROUGE, BERTScore)
Thorough analysis of error distributions and identification of temporal information loss challenges in fMRI-to-text decoding
Clear presentation of results with detailed tables, figures, and reproducibility details
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: side network is standard Transformer encoder-decoder; predictive coding attention is merely standard attention with a causal mask

Weak theory-practice connection: linear verification analysis (brain score) doesn't justify the nonlinear model design; acknowledged but unresolved tension with Antonello & Huth (2024) alternative explanation
Unclear mechanistic contribution: no clear explanation of why predicting future words (Vj) in a side network is superior to other ROI incorporation methods

Marginal improvements with unexplained attribution: ~5-8 BLEU-1 improvements don't reflect meaningful reconstruction gains (Table 8 case studies show incoherent outputs); information loss reduction may reflect temporal alignment rather than predictive coding

Insufficient statistical rigor: no significance testing, confidence intervals, or error bars; very small sample sizes (3 subjects on LeBel's); λ hyperparameter requires dataset-specific tuning without principled justification
Circular ROI selection: BPC regions pre-selected from literature; improvements over random ROIs demonstrate ROI selection matters, not that predictive coding framework is fundamentally superior

Inadequate evaluation: extremely low BLEU-2/3/4 scores indicate problem remains largely unsolved; authors acknowledge word-level evaluation is insufficient but don't implement proposed semantic-level evaluation
Incomplete ablations: only removes entire side network; doesn't test removing predictive coding attention mask, training without side loss, or using different ROIs with same architecture
Poor generalization of findings: only tested on language comprehension tasks; limited to two datasets with small sample sizes
Overstated novelty: title emphasizes brain predictive coding but model doesn't implement predictive coding mechanisms—merely processes ROIs that correlate with prediction

strengths: Strong theoretical motivation grounding fMRI-to-text decoding in well-established predictive coding theory from neuroscience, with empirical verification that brain signals encode predictive information

Comprehensive experimental validation across two datasets with both within-subject and cross-subject settings, multiple metrics, and thorough ablation studies demonstrating the side network's necessity
Consistent and meaningful improvements over strong baselines (e.g., 34.95% BLEU-1 vs 27.11% MapGuide on LeBel's), with particularly clear gains in BLEU-1 and ROUGE1-F
Insightful analysis connecting prediction length/distance effects to temporal scales of human prediction and demonstrating that BPC regions outperform random/whole-brain ROI selection
Detailed error analysis revealing information loss issues caused by fMRI's temporal resolution and showing PREDFT helps mitigate this through predictive signals

Excellent reproducibility with extensive implementation details, hyperparameters, and experimental protocols; includes appropriate controls (chance-level experiments) and honest limitations discussion
weaknesses: Limited architectural novelty: the model is a straightforward application of standard Transformers with attention-based fusion; the main contribution is applying existing predictive coding verification ideas to a downstream task

Problematic absolute performance: BLEU-1 scores of 34.95% drop sharply to 14.53% for BLEU-2 and become negligible at BLEU-3/4 (5.62%, 1.78%); case studies show frequent incoherence, limiting practical utility

Circular ROI verification: ROIs selected based on prior neuroscience knowledge are verified using the same fMRI data; more principled data-driven ROI discovery would strengthen claims and reduce overfitting to known anatomy

Insufficient mechanistic understanding: paper verifies predictive coding information exists but doesn't explain why the network learns to use it; unclear whether improvements come from genuine predictive coding or simply additional brain signal information

Weak cross-subject generalization: within-subject results (LeBel's) substantially outperform cross-subject results (Narratives), with modest improvements over UniCoRN (24.73% vs 20.64%); suggests individual prediction differences or limited transfer, not adequately analyzed
Hyperparameter sensitivity: λ varies by sequence length (1.0 vs 0.5) without principled justification; unclear if this requires per-setting tuning for new domains

Unresolved fundamental temporal mismatch: fMRI's low temporal resolution (0.5-0.67/sec sampling vs 3-5 words/sec speech rate) causes information loss; PREDFT helps partially but doesn't address the core limitation

Incomplete evaluation methodology: paper acknowledges BLEU/ROUGE inadequately capture semantics and suggests semantic-level metrics, but provides no quantitative semantic evaluation; undermines confidence in reported improvements

Unfair baseline comparisons: different methods use different pre-trained models (UniCoRN uses BART while PREDFT trains from scratch); PREDFT w/o SideNet sometimes outperforms baselines, suggesting gains may come from main network rather than side network
